To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

tri-bimaximal neutrino mixing is a possible outcome of low-scale inverse or linear seesaw models, with the inverse seesaw predicting a lower bound for the neutrinoless double decay decay rate, while the linear seesaw model does not, and that both scenarios predict lepton flavor violating decay rates of order 10-2-10-3.
the A4 flavor symmetric linear seesaw scheme leads to a lower limit on neutrinoless double-beta decay while the inverse scheme does not.

(1) the inverse and the linear seesaw can be embedded into A4-based scenarios with tri-bimaximal neutrino mixing; (2) the linear seesaw predicts a lower bound for the effective neutrinoless double-beta decay mass parameter; (3) the linear seesaws leads to potentially large branching ratios for lepton flavor violation processes, while the inverse seesaws does not.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the phenomenological aspects of low-scale seesaw models with A4 flavor symmetry.
the phenomenological consequences of a flavor symmetry in the lepton sector, which leads to the prediction of tri-bimaximal neutrino mixing.
the question whether low-scale seesaw scenarios can accommodate tri-bimaximal neutrino mixing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
these models are testable at the LHC, but the results are model dependent.
the A4-based linear seesaw model can be ruled out, while the inverse seesaws can be probed by LHC and neutrinoless double-beta decay experiments.
these models are highly predictive and testable at the LHC and in future neutrino oscillation experiments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the A4-based linear seesaw model is the most promising model among the two, with the A4-based inverse seesaw model being the second best.
, in the inverse seesaw, the LHC can probe the lepton flavor violating decay τ→μe, while in the linear seesaw the LHC can only probe the decay τ→μτ.
, in order to explain the observed lepton flavor mixing pattern, one may have to accept a large number of light neutrino mass states and a large number of lepton flavor violating decay rates.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the inverse seesaw is more flexible than the linear seesaw, in the sense that it can accommodate larger neutrino mass splittings, and thus can be tested by neutrino experiments, in particular the next generation of long-baseline experiments.
a large class of models can be ruled out at the LHC if the lightest neutrino is found to be massless, and if lepton flavor violating decays are observed.
the inverse and linear seesaws can lead to highly predictive models with TeV-scale physics that can be probed at the LHC.
